items.question: What is HeatAhead?
items.answer: HeatAhead uses weather and past building records to estimate where heating problems are more likely in NYC. You can check a building, explore the map or see which places may need an inspection. The score is an estimate, not a live check of the heating.

items.question: How do I check my building?
items.answer: Go to Check a building. Enter its street address and borough, or its 10-digit BBL, then choose Look up. You'll see the available risk score, complaint history and owner details. Leave out your apartment number.
terms: How can I check my building?

items.question: What is a BBL?
items.answer: A BBL is NYC's 10-digit property ID, short for Borough, Block and Lot. One ID can cover more than one building. If you don't know it, you can search using the street address instead.

items.question: How do I use the map?
items.answer: The map covers all five boroughs. Use the Minimum risk slider to hide lower scores, or Jump to an area to choose a borough. Switch between Flat map and 3D view. Zoom in to see colored dots for individual properties.
terms: How can I explore the risk map?

items.question: What happens when I click a hexagon?
items.answer: The city view uses larger hexagons so the map is easier to read. Zoom in to see smaller areas, then dots for individual properties. Click a hexagon to see its buildings, with higher scores first. Your current filter still applies. Use Next to see more, or Zoom to these buildings to look closer. Click a building in the list to open its record.

items.question: Why are some hexagons taller?
items.answer: Taller hexagons mean more heating complaints were recorded in that area last season. A few buildings with lots of complaints can make a tall hexagon. Height doesn't show how many buildings there are. When you zoom in, the gray building shapes and their heights come from the background map.

items.question: What do the map colors mean?
items.answer: Darker blue means higher estimated winter risk. A hexagon shows the average score of the properties inside it. When you zoom in, each colored dot shows one property's score. Height shows past complaints, which is a different measure.

items.question: What does winter risk mean?
items.answer: It's the estimated chance of a heating problem at some point this winter, based on the building's records. It doesn't tell you whether the heat is working right now. Open the building's page to see its score and history.

items.question: Why are the winter and cold-day scores different?
items.answer: Winter risk covers the whole season. Cold-day risk looks at a much shorter period around freezing weather. A building has more time to run into a problem over a whole winter, so the two scores can be quite different. Compare scores that cover the same period.
terms: How is cold-day risk different from winter risk?

items.question: How accurate are the scores?
items.answer: On a building's page, open How accurate is this number? It compares predictions with what happened in a winter that wasn't used to train the model. This helps check the model overall; it can't tell us for sure what will happen to one building. From 20% up, we show ranges, and no score goes above 99%.
terms: How can I check how accurate the estimates are?

items.question: Why do some buildings have no hexagons or color?
items.answer: The background map shows more buildings than we've scored. Some properties have missing records or map locations, and filters can hide lower scores. Some 3D hexagons stay flat because no complaints were recorded there last season. Try Flat map. When you zoom in, dots replace hexagons. A building without color can still have heating problems. Try resetting the filter or looking up its address.
terms: Why do some buildings have no hexagon or risk score?

items.question: Where does the information come from?
items.answer: We use public NYC records about buildings, heat complaints, violations, owners and boilers, along with weather data. Records can be missing or out of date. A complaint means someone reported a problem; it doesn't mean an inspector confirmed it.
terms: where does the information come from

items.question: What information do you keep about me?
items.answer: The map shows information about buildings, not individual tenants. Saving a building for alerts links it to your verified email address. Owner details come from public business records. Please leave passwords, email addresses, phone numbers and apartment numbers out of the guide chat.
terms: What personal information does HeatAhead use?

items.question: How do I sign up or sign in?
items.answer: Choose Sign in on the home page. When available, use Continue with Google or request an email sign-in link. The email link works once for 15 minutes. The same options create your account or sign you back in. If both are being set up, you can still check buildings and use the map without an account.
terms: How can I sign up or sign in?

items.question: Will I stay signed in when I come back?
items.answer: Tick Keep me signed in for 30 days on this device before signing in with Google or requesting an email link. Your browser may end the session sooner if you clear cookies or use stricter privacy settings. Use the same email address to find your saved buildings again. Sign out if you're on a shared device.

items.question: How do I get email alerts?
items.answer: When sign-in is available, sign in and find Save a building in your profile. Enter its street address and borough, or BBL, tick the email-alert box and choose Save to my account. Turn on My buildings & alerts to see saved buildings on your dashboard. Emails are sent for qualifying forecast cold spells when the team's alert service is running.
terms: How can I get cold-snap email alerts?

items.question: How do I stop alerts or remove a building?
items.answer: Sign in with the same email address you used to save the building. Turn on My buildings & alerts in your profile if needed. Under Your saved buildings, choose Stop alerts & remove. You can also use the unsubscribe link in an alert email and confirm the removal.
terms: How can I stop alerts or remove a saved building?

items.question: How can landlords use HeatAhead?
items.answer: Look up your building to check its history and available owner or agent details. Choose I own or manage it under Draft a notice to prepare a message about a heating check. If you sign in, you can turn on Landlord self-audit tools in your profile. That dashboard choice doesn't verify ownership.
terms: How can a landlord use HeatAhead?

items.question: How do I write a message about my building?
items.answer: On the building's page, find Draft a notice. Choose the tenant or landlord option, then click Draft the notice. Read and edit the message, then copy it or open your email app. You send it yourself. Owner records may list a mailing address rather than an email address.
terms: How can I draft a message about my building?

links.label: Find a building and draft a message

items.question: How do I find buildings to inspect?
items.answer: Open Inspection queue to see the first 50 building records in the saved cold-day model ranking. Each row links to its building and map, and you can download the same top 50 as a CSV. This snapshot is separate from winter risk and is not HPD’s official inspection schedule. Use Published complaints for recent reports or Historical model replay to see a past queue change.
terms: How can inspectors use the ranked queue?

items.question: Is the live monitor showing what's happening now?
items.answer: Published complaints shows recent heat reports released by NYC, with a delay. It refreshes every 15 seconds while the source is checked every five minutes; it doesn't confirm an outage is still active. Historical model replay is separate: it replays February 7–9, 2026 complaints to show rankings changing. Check the replay clock for its date. Building pages and the map still work if the monitor is offline.
terms: Is the live monitor showing events happening right now?

items.question: What should I do if I have no heat or hot water?
items.answer: Tell your landlord, superintendent or managing agent. If the problem isn't fixed, report it to NYC311. Give your contact and apartment details directly to NYC311. You don't need to wait for a high score or an email alert to report a heating problem.

links.label: Report a heat problem through NYC311

items.question: What are NYC's heating rules?
items.answer: NYC heat season runs from October 1 to May 31. From 6 AM to 10 PM, your home must be at least 68°F when it's below 55°F outside. From 10 PM to 6 AM, it must be at least 62°F, whatever the outdoor temperature. Hot water must reach at least 120°F all year. See HPD's page for the official rules.
terms: What are NYC’s heat and hot-water requirements?

sources.label: NYC HPD: heat and hot water

items.question: Are the building photos live?
items.answer: No. The aerial photos and Google Street View images were taken earlier, and their dates and coverage vary. Street View opens the closest available view. The location marker shows the property's mapped position. Gray building shapes come from the background map; they don't show whether the heating works.
terms: Are the building photos and shapes live?

items.question: Does a high score mean my heat will definitely fail?
items.answer: No. A higher score means the model thinks a heating problem is more likely, but it can't say for sure. Some problems never get reported, and records and forecasts can be wrong. Use the score to help decide what to check. A real heating problem should still be reported, whatever the score.
terms: Does a high score mean a building will definitely lose heat?

items.question: What if I smell gas or a carbon monoxide alarm sounds?
items.answer: Leave the building and call 911 from outside. HeatAhead can't send emergency help. For a heating problem without immediate danger, contact your landlord and NYC311.
terms: What if I smell gas or a carbon-monoxide alarm sounds?

items.question: How do I get or stop project updates?
items.answer: Project updates are separate from building heat alerts. Use the newsletter form near the bottom of the home page. Your email is required; your name is optional. You join after confirming the link in your email. To stop updates, open the unsubscribe link in a project-update email and confirm. This won't change your building alerts. If signup is being set up, try later or contact our team.

items.question: How do I contact the HeatAhead team?
items.answer: Email heataheadnyc@gmail.com with questions, feedback or corrections. A building's street address or BBL is enough; leave out apartment details, passwords and sign-in links. For a heating complaint, use NYC311. Our team inbox doesn't file reports or send inspectors.

items.question: How do I change my cookie choices?
items.answer: Choose Accept all, Reject optional or Settings in the cookie banner. You can reopen Cookie settings in the footer any time. Optional storage remembers dashboard choices on this device and starts off until you accept it. Rejecting it doesn't sign you out or remove saved buildings. Essential sign-in cookies stay on. HeatAhead doesn't use analytics or advertising cookies; the privacy page explains external map and photo services.
